newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS-Lyonnaise, Suez form utility power.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Lyonnaise, Suez form utility power.

text.p: French holding company Cie de Suez said on Friday it would ask a shareholders meeting to approve a merger with utility group Lyonnaise des Eaux and set a dividend three times last year's payout.

The Suez and Lyonnaise supervisory boards met to approve merger terms that will create a group with annual sales of some 200 billion francs ($34.5 billion) and have a market capitalisation of 75 billion francs.

Suez said in a statement its board decided to ask shareholders at a meeting to be held on June 11 to approve the merger terms and authorise a dividend of 24.60 francs a share, representing a total payout of 3.8 billion francs. It paid a dividend of 8.20 francs for 1995.
It will also ask for approval for a cancellation of the five percent of its issued capital currently held as treasury stock.
Under the deal, Suez shareholders will get 20 Lyonnaise shares for 41 Suez, a source close to the merger talks said.
Lyonnaise chairman Jerome Monod told Europe 1 radio that the larger group would absorb Suez, a financial services and utilities company, through a friendly "merger-takeover".
The combined group will focus on four core businesses -- energy, water distribution, waste management and communications.
Lyonnaise's "mission is to conquer the world", said Monod.

The companies, two of France's top corporate players, were due to announce at 1630 GMT on Friday details of the deal that will end the independence of Suez. It was set up in the 19th Century to build the Suez Canal, a glory of French engineering.
Trading in the two companies' shares was suspended on the Paris bourse on Friday ahead of the announcement.
The combined group, to be called Suez Lyonnaise des Eaux, would give shareholders "a very big world actor that will be a leader in its activities and enjoy high visibility", Monod said.
It would have the "resources to invest" around 17 billion francs from its first year of operation, he said.
Monod has promised that the merged group will boost profits and cashflow.
Lyonnaise, which has activities in water distribution, construction and communications, has been pushing the deal as an operation that will give it extra muscle to expand abroad.

But by focusing on the four core activities, analysts say Lyonnaise's construction activities and most of the financial and industrial holdings controlled by Suez -- apart from Belgian energy and services giant Tractebel -- could be up for sale.

Lyonnaise is twice the size of Suez in terms of shareholder funds and one third bigger in share capitalisation. Suez, once one of France's grandest corporate institutions, fell victim in the early 1990s to a property slump.

Disgruntled Suez shareholders forced out the previous chairman Gerard Worms after the group posted a four billion franc loss in 1995 and installed Gerard Mestrallet to turn round the overly diversified colossus.

Mestrallet swiftly sold crown jewels such as investment bank Banque Indosuez and fund manager Gartmore. he also disposed of the ailing real estate portfolio, leaving Suez with more than five billion francs in cash.
But he held on to a 63-percent stake in Belgian holding company, Societe Generale de Belgique, which groups some choice industrial and financial assets. ($ = 5.789 French Francs)
